# Spikes

Throwaway crates and scripts that answered the Spike 0 questions in
`docs/design.md` before any product code was written. Each directory has a
README with the commands run, their output, and a recommendation. They are
kept for reference and are not built by the main crate.

| Dir | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `01-claude-resume` | Can Claude Code sessions be captured and resumed? | Yes: `--session-id <uuid>` at launch, `--resume <uuid>` later from any terminal. Transcripts pruned after 30 days unless `cleanupPeriodDays` is raised. |
| `02-process-host` | tmux or own PTYs? | tmux on a private server: sessions outlive the app, reattach works, ~3 ms round trip. PTY adapter kept as fallback and for tests. |
| `03-session-state` | How to know "waiting on you"? | Claude Code hooks (`PermissionRequest`, `Stop`, `SessionEnd`) via a tiny `switchboard-hook` binary and a Unix socket; OSC 777 text from the raw stream as the hook-free fallback. |
| `05-keychain` | Can secrets live in the Keychain without prompts? | Yes for a bundle signed with a stable identity and identifier: the item ACL is `identifier + certificate`, so rebuilds read silently. Ad-hoc builds prompt per rebuild. |
| `06-pane-size` | Why is the embedded pane wider than the widget? | `window-size manual` ignored the client; `latest` makes the window follow whichever client attached last. Re-applied on launch for servers that outlive the app. |
| `07-clone-session` | Can a session be cloned up to a chosen message? | Yes: copy the transcript prefix before the chosen prompt, substitute a fresh UUID for `sessionId`, save it `0600` beside the original; `--resume <new>` opens the truncated history and the original is untouched. |
| `08-promptbox-embed` | Can Prompt Box be the agent message box? | Yes: same egui 0.36, drawn into a bottom panel unchanged, a `Clipboard` adapter turns Send into a hand-off; needs an embedded mode, a sink port, and focus-scoped shortcuts in promptbox. |
| `09-popout` | Can a session live in a window of its own? | Yes: an immediate viewport drawn from the main frame holds the page, terminal, and side panel; its frame is saved to settings and restored. |
| `10-nunchuk-serial` | Can a nunchuk drive the working set over USB serial? | Yes: one line per button change or stick flick from the Feather, read on a thread that reconnects; round trip 2 to 9 ms. Firmware in `firmware/nunchuk`. |
| `11-gate-sandbox` | Can Dispatch's pipeline commands be confined to the ticket's tree on macOS? | Yes: `sandbox-exec` with `(allow default)`, writes denied except the tree, the attempt directory, the lane's caches and a base set; ~5 ms start-up; a refused write is `EPERM` and a tagged `deny(1)` line in the unified log. `setuid` programs and keychain creation fail inside it. |
| `12-hidden-frames` | Does the frame loop keep running while the window is occluded or minimized? | Not before the fix: with the app hidden, a control query timed out after 10 s and was answered at once on unhide. With the tick and `pump` in `App::logic`, hidden queries answer in 75 to 103 ms (eframe's 100 ms throttle for invisible windows). The sleep and wake cycle is not yet measured. |
| `13-dispatch-service` | Can a Dispatch service be a Switchboard service session, and how is its port read? | Yes: `$SHELL -lc 'exec "$@"' dispatch-service env PORT=<port> npm start` finds `npm`, answers (CRA in 27 s), and is gone with its port 200 ms after `kill-session`. A port is free only if `0.0.0.0`, `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` all bind: CRA listens on `*`, which a loopback bind does not see. |
| `14-env-exec` | Do a pane's record id and launch token reach a child, so `switchboard-env exec` can resolve its sets? | Yes for a shell grandchild of a tmux pane started with `-e`; the binary's path is covered by `tests/control.rs`. The `aws-vault` form and the no-prompt run under Dispatch's launch flags were not run and are left to the owner. |
| `15-paste-buffer` | Can a multi-line send be bracketed only for a pane that asked for it? | Yes: `load-buffer -` then `paste-buffer -p -r -d` frames the text in `ESC[200~` .. `ESC[201~` for a pane with `bracket_paste_flag` 1 and delivers it bare otherwise; `-r` keeps LF, `-d` leaves no buffer. CR passes through and tmux 3.7c shows ESC as a literal `^[`, so the sender turns CR into LF and removes ESC. `send-keys -H` passes the markers to every pane. Measured on tmux 3.7c. |
| `16-base-pipeline` | Can Dispatch find a merged pull request's merge commit and read the base's pipeline on it? | GitHub, yes: `mergeCommit` on `gh pr list` and `gh pr view`, and the commit's `check-runs` (a short hash works) show the base's run in progress and then finished. Bitbucket's reads were not run (the token could not be read in the run); the adapter follows the documented `merge_commit.hash`, commit `statuses` and pipeline `steps`, with a read by number when a list row lacks the commit; until they are run, a wait on a Bitbucket base pipeline is refused. |
| `18-tmux-argv` | Do `new-session -e` values show in a process listing, and can they reach tmux another way? | Yes, they did: the server keeps the argv of the client that started it. `tmux start-server \; source-file -` with the `new-session` line on stdin keeps every value and the pane command off any argv; cold and warm both work, errors still return, and double-quoted values with `\n` for line breaks round-trip (single quotes lose a line starting with `#`). Measured on tmux 3.7c. |
| `19-structured-ask` | Does a card's answer to a structured ask reach interactive Claude Code as the next user message, sent once, both at the prompt and when held until the turn's `Stop`? | Yes: `Owner answered "<question>": <answer>`, typed as one line, arrived as its own user message once in both cases; a held answer went out only after the `Stop`. Measured on Claude Code 2.1.293 by the ignored gate test `a_structured_answer_arrives_as_the_next_prompt`. |
| `21-evidence-writes` | Which writes reach a stage's evidence directory, outside the agent's cwd, without a prompt? | The Write tool, under the attempt directory's `Edit(//<dir>/**)` rule. Bash `cp`, `mv` and `mkdir` ask, and `--add-dir` does not change that. A Playwright MCP screenshot is refused outside the server's roots unless it runs with `--allow-unrestricted-file-access`. Measured on Claude Code 2.1.295 and `@playwright/mcp@0.0.82`. |
| `22-remote-port` | Can a pinned-TLS HTTP and WebSocket port run on std with every request answered by the frame thread, and what does it cost? | Yes: `rustls` + `rcgen` + `tungstenite` + `mdns-sd`, no Tokio; the frame's share is under 0.25 ms per pass, latency is one frame interval, the pools and the subscriber overflow hold under a stall and an unread socket, Bonjour is seen by `dns-sd`. A 146 MB transcript parses in 290 ms at 575 MB peak, so content work leaves the frame thread. ctime and inode see the file changes mtime and size miss. |
| `04-terminal-view` | Embedded terminal or hand-off? | Hand off agents to Ghostty (`open -na Ghostty --args ... -e cmd`, raise by title); embed `egui_term` for shells, commands, services. |

Findings are folded into `docs/design.md` under "Spike 0 results".

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). Web search results for query: "WebSocket cookie sent on upgrade request SameSite Strict HttpOnly Secure self-signed certificate Safari Chrome"

Links: [{"title":"WebKit Bugzilla","url":"https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=232666"},{"title":"Cookie not sent on websocket","url":"https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/104488"},{"title":"show bug","url":"https://bugzilla.cendio.com/show_bug.cgi?id=5978"},{"title":"Cross-Site WebSocket Hijacking Exploitation in 2025","url":"https://blog.includesecurity.com/2025/04/cross-site-websocket-hijacking-exploitation-in-2025/"},{"title":"WebKit Bugzilla","url":"https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=200345"},{"title":"Intent to Prototype: Schemeful Same-Site","url":"https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/qB7DKqxkiaA/m/IEqPn3RYDgAJ"},{"title":"XSRF-TOKEN can not be set in Safari 17.0 over IPv6","url":"https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/770644"},{"title":"作者:Sebastian Gingter","url":"https://blog.51cto.com/biyusr/5530775"},{"title":"WebKit Bugzilla","url":"https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345"}]

The search turned up reports that Safari can drop SameSite=Strict cookies on WebSocket upgrades, but nothing that covers your exact combination of self-signed certificate, Secure cookie, and Safari versus Chrome.

- **Safari drops Strict cookies on WebSocket requests.** A WebKit bug report says Strict cookies were not sent over WebSocket in restored or history-loaded tabs, while XHR requests still got them. The reporter saw it on Safari 14 and 15, and believed it was fixed in 15.1. SameSite Strict cookies are not sent via WebSocket on any restored/cache-loaded tabs
- **Your exact symptom matches a developer report.** An Apple forum post describes cookies set on a 101 upgrade response with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Strict that were not sent on the next connection in Safari. Removing HttpOnly made Safari work, while Chrome and Firefox worked with the flags intact. The above setup works fine on Chrome/Firefox.
- **Self-signed certificates add a separate Safari problem.** One report says Safari doesn't let us use WebSockets by default when using a self-signed certificate. The user must approve the certificate manually, and a declined certificate produces no useful error. A WebKit bug also notes that Chrome and Safari would not accept a self-signed cert without a Subject Alternative Name (SAN).
- **Chrome's Strict behavior is different.** Chrome's schemeful same-site change affects cookies across http and https schemes, which is relevant if your self-signed setup mixes schemes.

Caveat: none of these sources tests a self-signed cert with Secure, HttpOnly, and Strict cookies together in Safari. The cookie-drop reports are mostly from 2019–2021, so current Safari behavior needs checking. The safest first step is to test with a trusted certificate, or check whether Safari has manually approved the cert, before concluding the cookie is the cause.


REMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.

Fette","url":"https://ietf.org/rfc/rfc6455"},{"title":"oneuptime.com","url":"https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-24-websocket-protocol-error/view"},{"title":"www.rfc-editor.org","url":"https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc6455.html"},{"title":"B4J Question Web socket server - fail connect clients with header \"Sec-WebSocket-Protocol\"","url":"https://www.b4x.com/android/forum/threads/web-socket-server-fail-connect-clients-with-header-sec-websocket-protocol.148619/?amp=1"},{"title":"[Bug 23576] New: Clarify what to do when received null value subprotocol in reply to non-empty subprotocol","url":"https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-webapps/2013OctDec/0229.html"},{"title":"greenbytes.de","url":"https://greenbytes.de/tech/specs/rfc6455.pdf"}]

The search suggests your premise is only partly right. The RFC doesn't require the server to echo a subprotocol, but browsers can refuse the connection when the client offered subprotocols and the server answers without one.

- **RFC 6455 allows omission:** A WebSocket-Python maintainer quoted the RFC as letting the server decline a requested subprotocol by not returning the header. The RFC 6455 seems to say that the server may decide not to acknowledge the requested subprotocol by not returning a Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header.
- **Browsers fail anyway:** Chrome 30+ users reported handshake errors with a "Sec-WebSocket-Protocol mismatch" message, and some developers worked around it by removing the header entirely. In one thread, setting a subprotocol on the server allows a Chrome connection to be made without issue.
- **Spec ambiguity:** A W3C bug report (23576) argues that this text adds a requirement that a WebSocket client MUST abort connection establishment if the peer server doesn't select any subprotocol offered by the client. The reporter notes that RFC 6455 itself doesn't require a client to abort connection establishment. The bug proposes that the user agent fail the connection in that case. I couldn't confirm from these results whether that change was adopted.
- **Disagreement on fault:** One commenter argued that if Chrome fails because the header is missing, then it's Chrome's fault I believe. Another replied that Chrome does the right thing here as per the client-side API of WebSocket.

Practical takeaway: if a client sends `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` and the server doesn't pick one, browsers may close the connection. The fix is to return one of the offered protocols in the handshake response, or to stop sending the header when the server doesn't support subprotocols. The sources here are mostly forum threads and a bug tracker, so check the current WHATWG WebSocket API text before relying on the browser behavior.

Safari's default WebSocket framework on **iOS, iPadOS, and ARM-based Macs** doesn't support the WebSocket Secure sessions Cockpit needs when using a self-signed or invalid certificate, even if you mark it as trusted. The recommended fix is installing a valid certificate. The alternative is enabling Apple's experimental WebSocket framework, labeled "NSURLSession WebSocket."

**Workaround:**
- **iOS/iPadOS:** Go to Settings > Safari > Advanced > Experimental Features, then turn on "NSURLSession WebSocket."
- **macOS on ARM (M1):** Enable "Show Develop menu in menu bar" in Safari's Advanced settings. Then, in the Develop menu, select Experimental Features and enable "NSURLSession WebSocket."

For the self-signed certificate part, the likely explanation is that Safari shows a certificate warning and refuses to load an HTTPS page on a raw IP and port until you accept the risk. content.content:
**Subprotocol rule:** If the client offered subprotocols and the server's response doesn't acknowledge one, the connection fails. The spec says the connection fails when "the empty byte sequence, then fail the WebSocket connection." This check goes beyond the WebSocket Protocol's own rule, which only covers a subprotocol the client never requested: "This covers a subprotocol requested by the client, but not acknowledged by the server."

**Cookies:** The spec doesn't state directly whether cookies are sent. It builds the handshake request with a "credentials mode" of "`include`," and delegates request handling to the Fetch Standard, which governs cookie behavior. So the handshake is intended to carry credentials, but this document doesn't spell out the cookie details.

The search turned up a known WebKit discrepancy: Safari doesn't always match `wss://` WebSocket URLs against `connect-src 'self'`, while Chrome and Firefox do.

- **The Safari bug:** WebKit Bugzilla report 201591 describes a service worker with `connect-src 'self'` that Safari blocks from opening a WebSocket on its own host and port. One commenter confirmed that the behavior works as intended in Chrome and Firefox but not Safari, and a later comment said it was still unfixed in Safari 14. The report links a Chromium issue that was fixed earlier, along with a related W3C CSP issue.
- **The spec question:** The W3C CSP issue #7 explains the root cause. Since WebSocket connections are not same-origin requests, a CSP with connect-src 'self' will not allow websockets back to the same host/port. The thread considered either documenting this as intended or adding an exception for same host/port WebSocket URLs.
- **MDN's position:** MDN's connect-src reference lists WebSocket among the APIs this directive controls, and notes that connect-src 'self' does not resolve to websocket schemes in all browsers.

**Summary: Safari doesn't send cookies on WebSocket reconnects, and the thread has no resolution.**

# Facts for issue #230 (web control surface)

No spike was run: every open question left is a real-browser or real-device question, which cannot run here (no iPhone, no Safari with a LAN bind). Git status is clean.

## Settled

### The tree

- The certificate has **no subjectAltName**: `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())` and only a CommonName `Switchboard <server_id>`. `src/adapters/remote.rs:95-120` (`make_identity`). Not for the LAN IP or any hostname.
- `respond` writes only `Content-Type: application/json`, `Content-Length`, `Connection`; the status reason table has no 302/304/405-other. `respond_upgrade` writes the 101 by hand with no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, so a subprotocol echo is a one-line additive change. `src/adapters/remote.rs:519-553`.
- `read_request` drops `cookie`, `user-agent`, `origin`, `host`, `sec-websocket-protocol`; `RemoteRequest` (360-372) and `RemoteReply` (389-393: status, body, authenticated) have no header fields. Cookie auth, a user-agent device name, a `Set-Cookie` on the pair reply, or static-file headers each need additive fields. (Investigation notes 18-19, 26.)
- Rate windows key on exact `PAIR_PATH`/`INFO_PATH` only (`Limits::limited`, 633-640); static paths are unlimited and count only against the 4-slot unauthenticated pool (568, 696-706) until a reply with `authenticated` promotes the connection (843-858).
- `serve_remote` refuses anything without the `/api/v1/` prefix as 404 `not_found` (`src/app.rs:3023`). `tests/remote.rs:682` (`the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else...`) only exercises `/api/v1/...` paths, so a new `GET /` does not break it. No test in `tests/remote.rs` or `src/adapters/remote.rs` uses a bare `/` path or `HEAD`/`OPTIONS` (grep). The plan must define HEAD/OPTIONS/trailing slash for the new routes; today they fall to 404.
- Revocation: a removed device's next request is 401 `unauthorized` "the token is not known; pair again" (`src/app.rs:3145`). Key rotation deletes all device records (`docs/remote-client.md` §5, line 315), so a stale token after rotation gives the same 401. Only `/info` (unauthenticated, carries `spki_sha256`/`server_id`) tells them apart: the page must compare `/info` after a 401 to say "identity changed" versus "revoked". Spec line 315/317: client shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing.
- Events: metadata kinds `project`, `space`, `set`, `session` and collections `projects`, `sessions` (id = project), `waiting`, etc. arrive on `/api/v1/events` with **no `watch` frame**; `watch`/`unwatch` is only for content kinds `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output`, `file`. `docs/remote-client.md:240,256`. So "a session starts waiting and moves to top" needs only `changed {waiting}` / `changed {session}` plus a refetch of `waiting`; the last response needs `watch {conversation}` (it is a projection of that key, line 207), and the screen needs `watch {screen}`. A visible content view also refetches every 30 s (line 256). `scope=all` only adds Dispatch worker records (`src/app.rs:246-272`).
- `last_message` (the card's one-line excerpt) is a field of the session's metadata and moves with `changed {session}`, not with `conversation` (spec line 207).
- Only Claude Code sessions have a conversation; other kinds answer "no conversation" and the client falls back to `screen` (line 206): the issue's "last response or screen" split is the API's own.
- The QR payload is built in `src/ui/remote.rs:160-166` from `remote::local_address()` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962`); the address may be empty (loopback). `PairingInvite.parse` in Swift is `Wire.decode` of JSON only (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:94-117`).
- The code is Crockford, the key is hex, the id a UUID: none needs percent-decoding, so `read_request`'s undecoded query holds (`RemoteRequest::query` doc). `refuse` logs the path without the query.

### Outside the tree

**1. A WebSocket handshake to a host reached through a self-signed certificate is not reliable in Safari on iOS/iPadOS/Apple-silicon macOS even after the user clicks through.**
Cockpit's own docs: Safari's default WebSocket framework on iOS, iPadOS and ARM Macs does not support `wss://` with a self-signed or invalid certificate even when marked trusted; the workaround it ships is Settings > Safari > Advanced > Experimental Features > "NSURLSession WebSocket", or a valid certificate. https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari . Corroborated by WebKit bug 41419 (open since 2010: Safari honours the HTTPS click-through but not for `wss://`) https://www2.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419 . Two agreeing sources, no contradiction found; the Cockpit page names no iOS version, so the evidence covers "as of the page's current text, checked 2026-10-22". Consequence: the page needs a non-WebSocket fallback on Safari (poll `/api/v1/waiting` etc. on an interval, or `changed` by long poll); the WebSocket cannot be the only live path for the iPhone case in the acceptance text.
Queries: "WebSocket cookie sent on upgrade request SameSite Strict HttpOnly Secure self-signed certificate Safari Chrome"; "Safari iOS self-signed certificate visit this website Secure cookies not stored WebSocket wss fails after accepting certificate".

**2. A browser fails a WebSocket whose 101 does not acknowledge a subprotocol the page offered.**
WHATWG WebSockets standard: if the client offered subprotocols and the response's `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` is absent/not one offered, fail the connection (stricter than RFC 6455, which lets the server omit it). https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ . Chrome reports match (Adobe/Lawouach threads, leads only). So a subprotocol token design must echo exactly one offered value in `respond_upgrade`; the standard's token grammar admits base64url/hex.
Queries: "RFC 6455 Sec-WebSocket-Protocol server must echo subprotocol browser fails connection if missing".

**3. CSP `connect-src 'self'` does not cover same-host `wss:` in all browsers (Safari/WebKit).**
MDN note citing w3c/webappsec-csp#7: "`connect-src 'self'` does not resolve to websocket schemes in all browsers" https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/connect-src ; WebKit bug 201591 (service worker, Safari ≤14 unfixed) https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=201591 . Two agreeing sources. Build to `connect-src 'self' wss:` (MDN's own example form); this adds no external host because the page is served by a host that is also the only wss target.
Query: "Content-Security-Policy connect-src 'self' does not match wss WebSocket Safari".

**4. Safari has dropped `SameSite=Strict` cookies on WebSocket upgrades, and one report has `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookies not sent on a Safari WebSocket while Chrome/Firefox send them.**
WebKit bug 232666 (Strict cookies not sent on WebSocket in restored tabs, Safari 14/15, believed fixed 15.1) https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=232666 ; Apple forum thread 104488 (HttpOnly removal made Safari work; no version, no reply) https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/104488 . The second is a lead (single forum post) and unresolved; the first is a vendor bug that is reportedly fixed. Together with fact 1 this settles only that **cookie-on-upgrade in Safari is an observed risk with no vendor statement it is safe**; it does not settle the current behaviour (see Unresolved U1).
Query: same as fact 1.

**5. Chrome ≥58 matches the host only against the SAN, never the CommonName.**
Forum agreement (Graylog, NethServer, TrueNAS, Palo Alto) and WebKit bug 158345 (Chrome and Safari would not accept a self-signed cert without a SAN) https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345 ; Cendio bug 7401 (iOS 13 needs SAN, EKU, validity under 3 years) https://bugzilla.cendio.com/show_bug.cgi?id=7401 . The current cert has no SAN (above) and a year-4096 validity, so a browser reaching it by IP gets a name-mismatch error, and per one Palo Alto article Chrome may not offer "Proceed" for a missing SAN (other users report it does; not settled). iOS 13+ also rejects validity over ~825 days for non-root trust (Cendio). Build to: the identity gains a SAN for the address the URL carries, which means the certificate is re-made on address change or the SAN lists every private interface address plus the Bonjour `.local` name; this changes `identity.json`'s certificate and thus the pinned SPKI only if the key is regenerated (it need not be: the SPKI is of the key).
Queries: "Chrome self-signed certificate without subjectAltName ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID IP address URL proceed anyway allowed".

**6. iOS Camera opens a QR's web link in Safari from a notification banner showing the URL (iOS 11+).** https://www.iclarified.com/60903/ios-11-camera-app-recognizes-qr-codes/amp , https://thehackernews.com/2018/03/ios-qr-code-camera.html (hostname-parsing flaw with crafted `@`/port text; our URL has neither `@` nor userinfo). Nothing found on IP-literal hosts, ports or self-signed hosts being refused before Safari; the Camera hands the URL to Safari, which then shows the certificate page. Queries: "iPhone Camera app QR code https URL IP address port self-signed certificate opens Safari notification". Android is not covered.

## Unresolved

**U1. Does current Safari (iOS 26-class, macOS 26-class) carry a `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie, set by a fetch response on a click-through page, on `fetch` and on `new WebSocket()`?**
Tried: the three searches under facts 1 and 4 plus fetching the Apple thread; found only 2021-era and undated reports. Why not settled: no source states current behaviour. Line to build to: **favourable** (cookie works): the plan may use the cookie for `fetch` and WebSocket. **Unfavourable**: the plan must still keep the bearer header for native clients, send the token for the page's `fetch` in an `Authorization` header from memory/`sessionStorage`, and use the `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` token (echoing it) or authenticate the first WebSocket frame; it must also carry the polling fallback of fact 1. The plan should build the WebSocket path so one transport (subprotocol or first-frame auth) works without cookies, and treat a cookie as an addition only if the owner confirms it (O1).

**U2. Whether an iOS Safari click-through exception covers `fetch` from the page and persists (how long).** Tried: same queries; Cockpit says the HTTPS page works after trust but WebSocket does not. No source gives the duration. Build to: the page treats a failed `fetch` with no HTTP status as "unreachable or certificate not trusted" and says so; it never assumes the exception outlives a session. Favourable: nothing extra. Unfavourable: the pairing window's text names the warning as repeating.

**U3. Whether Chrome/Android offers "Proceed" for a certificate with no SAN, and whether Android camera/Lens opens an IP:port https URL.** Tried: query under fact 5 and 6; sources disagree or are silent. Build to: add the SAN regardless (fact 5); that makes the Chrome case equal to the ordinary self-signed case.

**U4. Whether a Firefox/Chrome page whose query was removed by `history.replaceState` before any request still has the code in the browser history or the camera app's own history.** The camera app and the first `GET /?code=...` request exist before the script runs, so the code reaches the host once and may sit in the camera app's or the OS's history. Not settleable by search. Build to: the code is single-use and the window closes after the pair (spec §5), so a leaked URL is dead after pairing and after five minutes; the plan says so in the dialog and does not claim more.

## For the owner

**O1. On the owner's iPhone/iPad (state the iOS version) and a Mac browser: after scanning the QR and clicking through the warning, does the page load, does `wss://` to the same host connect, and does a cookie set by the `/pair` fetch come back on the next `fetch`?**
Branch works in both cases: build the page with the `Authorization` header token held in memory/`sessionStorage` for `fetch`, the subprotocol-or-first-frame token for the socket, and a poll fallback every few seconds when the socket cannot open. If the owner reports the cookie works, the plan may swap `sessionStorage` for the HttpOnly cookie; if the socket works, the poll becomes a fallback only.

**O2. Do any of the owner's networks isolate wifi clients, or does the phone's camera app refuse the URL (and what does its banner show)?** Works in both cases: the page and the pairing window's text assume nothing about reachability beyond "the same network"; an unreachable host shows the unreachable state of U2.

**O3. Android: does Chrome offer "Proceed" and does the camera open `https://<ip>:<port>/?...`?** Only matters if the owner has an Android device; the plan builds the SAN either way.

No test in `tests/remote.rs` or `src/adapters/remote.rs` uses a bare `/` path or `HEAD`/`OPTIONS` (grep). The plan must define HEAD/OPTIONS/trailing slash for the new routes; today they fall to 404.
- Revocation: a removed device's next request is 401 `unauthorized` "the token is not known; pair again" (`src/app.rs:3145`). Key rotation deletes all device records (`docs/remote-client.md` §5, line 315), so a stale token after rotation gives the same 401. Only `/info` (unauthenticated, carries `spki_sha256`/`server_id`) tells them apart: the page must compare `/info` after a 401 to say "identity changed" versus "revoked". Spec line 315/317: client shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing.
- Events: metadata kinds `project`, `space`, `set`, `session` and collections `projects`, `sessions` (id = project), `waiting`, etc. arrive on `/api/v1/events` with **no `watch` frame**; `watch`/`unwatch` is only for content kinds `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output`, `file`. `docs/remote-client.md:240,256`.
